title: Is PMI Membership Worth It? (The Actual Maths)
dek: If you're about to sit a PMI exam, yes — the membership costs $139 and cuts the PMP fee by $250, so it pays for itself immediately. If you're only keeping it for the renewal discount afterwards, the maths stops working.

seo.metaDescription: The maths on PMI membership — when it pays for itself, when it doesn't, and why the renewal discount alone isn't a reason to keep paying.

sources.label: PMI — How to maintain your certification

body.richText: We spend a lot of time on this site telling people not to buy things. So it's worth being equally clear when something genuinely adds up — and for anyone about to sit a PMI exam, membership is one of the few upsells in this industry where the arithmetic is unambiguous.

The short answer: if you're taking the PMP or CAPM, join first. Membership costs $139 a year plus a small one-time application fee, and it cuts the PMP exam fee by $250. You're better off from day one, before counting anything else you get.
This is the whole argument in one table. Prices vary by region and PMI adjusts them periodically, so confirm your own figures — but the shape of it holds.

body.caption: Cost of taking the PMP with and without membership (2026 figures; confirm current fees with PMI).

body.richText: So you pay less overall and still hold a year's membership. That's why almost everyone taking a PMI exam joins first — and why not joining is usually just an oversight rather than a decision.

items: A digital copy of the PMBOK Guide, which you'd otherwise buy
Free webinars and on-demand courses that count toward PDUs and the 35 contact hours
Access to PMI's library of standards and research
Local chapter membership and events, which is where the networking actually happens
A reduced certification renewal fee — about $60 instead of $150

body.richText: The free PDU-earning webinars are the most underrated item on that list. Renewal requires 60 PDUs every three years, and members can cover a large share of them at no cost — which matters if the alternative was buying a PDU bundle. We explain how that works in our renewal guide.

Here's the part nobody mentions, and it's the reason this article exists rather than just repeating the sales pitch. The exam discount is a one-off. Once you're certified, the recurring comparison looks quite different:

body.caption: The recurring maths after you're certified.
rows: Membership costs far more than it saves on renewal

body.richText: Read plainly: the renewal discount alone is not a reason to keep paying. Roughly $30 a year of saving against $139 a year of cost is a losing trade. If you stay a member, stay for the webinars, the library and the chapter — things you'd actually use — not because you believe the renewal discount covers it. It doesn't.

A practical consequence: if you let membership lapse and later need to renew your certification, you'll pay the higher non-member renewal fee. That's fine and often still cheaper than a year of membership — just don't be surprised by it, and don't rejoin in a panic assuming you're saving money.

body.caption: A straight answer by situation.
rows: About to sit the PMP or CAPM
Join — it costs less than not joining
Certified, and you use the webinars for PDUs
Certified, active in a local chapter
Certified, but you never log in

items.question: How much does PMI membership cost?
items.answerRichText: $139 a year, plus a small one-time application fee for new members. Prices vary by region and PMI adjusts them periodically, so confirm the current figure for your country on PMI's site before joining.

items.question: Does PMI membership save money on the PMP exam?
answerRichText: Yes, and by more than the membership costs. The member exam fee is $405 against $655 for non-members — a saving of $250 against a membership of $139, so joining first leaves you $111 better off overall. See our

items.question: Should I keep PMI membership after getting certified?
answerRichText: Only if you use it. The renewal discount is worth about $90 once every three years against roughly $417 of membership over the same period, so it doesn't pay for itself. Keep it for the free PDU webinars, the library and chapter events — see
